cases.name: necroprinting
cases.title: Engineers Turn a Dead Mosquito Into the World's Finest 3D-Printing Nozzle
cases.body:
A small materials-engineering lab outside Portland has spent the past eighteen months trying to solve a problem that sounds almost absurd: how do you print a line of material narrower than a human hair without spending tens of thousands of dollars on custom-machined hardware? Their answer, published this week in a paper the team is calling only a preliminary technical note, is to stop machining anything at all and instead reach for a mosquito.

The insight came from an unlikely place. A postdoctoral researcher on the team, idly reading about insect anatomy during a slow afternoon, noticed that a mosquito's proboscis — the needle-like mouthpart it uses to pierce skin — tapers to a tip only a few hundred nanometers wide. Evolution shaped that taper over millions of years for a single purpose: sliding into skin and capillaries with as little pain and tissue damage as possible, so the insect can feed undetected. A machinist trying to grind a metal nozzle down to a comparable taper would need equipment costing more than the rest of the lab's budget combined, and even then the result would be blunter and more irregular than what a mosquito manages by default.

So the team tried something unconventional. They anesthetized and later preserved a small batch of lab-reared mosquitoes, carefully dissected out the proboscis from each one under a stereo microscope, and mounted the cleanest specimens into a custom-machined steel collar sized to hold the base of the mouthpart rigidly in place. The collar itself was unremarkable — a fairly ordinary piece of turned metal with a threaded fitting that could be screwed onto a standard syringe-pump extruder. The only exotic part of the whole assembly was the dead insect's mouth.

Once mounted, the researchers ran a UV-curable resin through the makeshift nozzle at low pressure and printed a series of test lines onto glass slides, curing each line with a handheld UV lamp as it emerged. Under a scanning electron microscope, the printed lines measured as narrow as 400 nanometers across — about half the width of the previous record, which had been set by a machined tungsten nozzle that took a specialty shop nearly three weeks to produce and cost several thousand dollars. The mosquito-derived nozzle, by contrast, cost the team essentially nothing beyond the insects themselves and a few hours of dissection work.

The lead engineer on the project, who asked that the lab's exact affiliation not be named until the technical note clears peer review, said the appeal isn't just the novelty. "We're not claiming this replaces industrial nozzle manufacturing," she said. "But for a research group that needs one or two ultra-fine test prints and doesn't have six months and a machine shop budget, this is a real option. It's also just a nice reminder that biology already solved some of these fabrication problems long before we did."

The technique, which the team has taken to calling "necroprinting" in internal notes, is not without limitations. The mounted proboscis is extremely fragile and typically survives only a handful of print runs before the tip fractures or clogs; the team reports needing three to five backup specimens on hand for any serious printing session. Flow rate through the tiny channel is also far lower than in a conventional nozzle, meaning a single test line can take several minutes to lay down. And because every proboscis is a little different, each mounted nozzle needs to be individually calibrated under a microscope before use, with the operator nudging the collar's alignment screws while watching resin bead at the tip.

Even so, the team believes the approach could find a niche in microelectronics prototyping and in early-stage medical-implant research, where a lab might need to print a handful of extremely fine conductive or biocompatible lines without committing to expensive custom tooling. They are now testing whether proboscises from other biting insects — certain species of biting midges and sand flies among them — taper even finer, and whether a chemically hardened coating could extend a mounted specimen's working life beyond a handful of runs.

cases.name: bridge_late_numeric_fact
cases.title: Portland Harbor Truss Bridge Reopens With Old Steel and a New Deck
cases.body:
The Portland Harbor Truss Bridge, a century-old steel structure that carries commuter traffic across the harbor channel, reopened to vehicles this week after a fourteen-month rehabilitation project that replaced its deck, repainted its trusses, and reinforced dozens of fatigue-prone connection points identified during a 2023 inspection.

The project's origins trace back to that inspection, when engineers from the regional transportation authority found hairline cracking in several of the bridge's lower chord connections — the joints where diagonal support beams meet the horizontal members that carry the roadway's weight. None of the cracks were judged to pose an immediate safety risk, but the authority opted to close two of the bridge's four lanes and begin a full rehabilitation rather than wait for a more serious failure to develop.

Crews began by stripping the bridge's original 1920s-era concrete deck down to the steel stringers beneath it, a process that took almost four months longer than planned after workers discovered unexpectedly extensive corrosion on several support beams near the bridge's midpoint. Replacing those beams required custom-fabricated steel sections, since the original manufacturer's specifications had been lost decades ago and new pieces had to be reverse-engineered from field measurements.

Once the underlying structure was stabilized, the project moved into its most visible phase: pouring a new lightweight concrete deck reinforced with corrosion-resistant rebar, designed to shave nearly 200 tons off the bridge's total dead load compared with the deck it replaced. Engineers say the weight reduction alone should meaningfully extend the service life of the aging truss below it, since much of the original fatigue damage was linked to decades of a heavier-than-necessary road surface.

The rehabilitation also included sandblasting and repainting the entire truss structure, replacing roughly 14,000 corroded rivets and bolts with new high-strength fasteners, and installing a modern expansion-joint system designed to better accommodate the bridge's thermal movement across the region's wide seasonal temperature swings. A new LED lighting system was added along the walkway on the bridge's north side, though officials note it was a minor add-on funded separately from the main structural contract.

The total cost of the rehabilitation came in at $42.7 million, funded primarily through a combination of federal bridge-preservation grants and regional transportation bonds. Despite the four-month delay caused by the unexpected corrosion discovery, the project's general contractor says the crew ultimately made up the lost time by running two shifts through the final phase of deck pouring and finished the entire rehabilitation eleven weeks ahead of the revised schedule that had accounted for the corrosion setback.

"We lost time early and made it back late," the project's site supervisor said at the reopening ceremony. "Nobody expected to beat the schedule after that midpoint delay, but the crews pushed hard through the summer and got it done." The bridge is now expected to remain in service, with only routine maintenance, for at least another forty years.
cases.question: How far ahead of the revised schedule did the crews finish?

cases.name: owls_named_person_fact
cases.title: Urban Owl Numbers Have Quietly Fallen by a Third, New Survey Finds
cases.body:
A five-year survey of barn owls and screech owls across a dozen midsize cities has found that nesting pairs have declined by roughly a third since monitoring began, a drop researchers describe as sharper and more consistent than they initially expected when the project started.

The survey combined nest-box monitoring, volunteer-reported sightings, and acoustic recorders placed in parks and cemeteries across the study cities to track owl activity over five consecutive breeding seasons. Early results in the first two years showed only modest year-to-year fluctuation, the kind researchers typically attribute to normal population noise rather than a genuine trend. It wasn't until the third and fourth seasons that the decline became statistically unmistakable, with several previously reliable nest sites going completely unused for two years running.

Dr. Naomi Castellanos, the ecologist who led the analysis, said the team spent most of the project's third year trying to rule out simpler explanations before accepting the more troubling one. "Our first assumption was that we were just getting worse at finding the owls, not that there were fewer of them," she said. "We checked observer turnover, we checked whether volunteers were covering the same sites consistently, we checked equipment failures on the acoustic recorders. None of that explained a drop this size."

After ruling out those confounds, Castellanos and her team turned to environmental data collected alongside the owl surveys. The clearest correlate they found was a rise in nighttime light levels across the study cities, driven largely by a wave of municipal LED streetlight conversions that occurred during the survey period. Owls hunt primarily by sound, locating small prey by the faint noises they make moving through grass or leaf litter, and rely on darkness to approach undetected. Brighter, whiter LED lighting, the team argues, both reduces the owls' ability to hunt undetected and appears to disrupt the low-light conditions rodents themselves prefer, pushing prey activity into darker, less accessible corners of the same parks.

"Light pollution disrupting nocturnal hunting patterns is the strongest single factor we found, though we're careful to call it a strong correlate rather than a proven sole cause," Castellanos said. The team also noted secondary contributors, including a reduction in the large dead trees that cavity-nesting owls prefer, as older urban trees are increasingly removed for safety reasons before they can develop natural nesting hollows.

The survey did not track or estimate the project's funding sources in its published methodology, and the research team's public summary does not mention who paid for the monitoring equipment or the volunteer coordination effort. Castellanos said only that the project "relied on a mix of institutional and volunteer support" without elaborating further in the released report.

The researchers are now recommending that cities piloting further LED conversions consider warmer color temperatures and adaptive dimming schedules in parks and cemeteries with known owl activity, changes they say could be implemented without materially affecting the lighting's usefulness for pedestrians.
cases.question: Who led the research?
